<!-- generated from skills/integrations-payments/subscriptions/SKILL.md (bundle form) -->

# subscriptions

## Metadata

- **Owner department:** D11 Integrations & Payments (IN)
- **Skill version:** 1.0.0
- **Last verified:** 2026-11-21
- **Sources:** Stripe, "Subscription invoices" — https://docs.stripe.com/billing/invoices/subscription ; Stripe, "Use free trial periods on subscriptions" — https://docs.stripe.com/billing/subscriptions/trials/free-trials ; Stripe, "Receive Stripe events in your webhook endpoint" — https://docs.stripe.com/webhooks
- **Depends on:** payments, webhooks
- **Feeds into:** dunning, refunds-disputes, invoicing-tax

## When to use / Do NOT use

- **Use when:** a product sells recurring access — trials, renewals, plan changes, pauses, cancellation — and the entitlement a user sees must match what the payment provider will actually charge. This skill owns the subscription lifecycle as mirrored from the provider.
- **Do NOT use when:** the charge is one-off (payments), the work is recovering a failed renewal (dunning), or money is moving back to the customer (refunds-disputes). Do not use it to design pricing; prices come from the catalog the billing configuration mirrors.

## Rules

1. **IN-021 — The provider state machine is the model.** Local subscription status mirrors the provider lifecycle (trialing, active, past_due, canceled/unpaid). Every local transition is driven by an invoice or subscription webhook event or a verified server-side API read — nothing else moves state.
2. **IN-022 — No local timers.** No local clock, cron job, client flag, or stored date ever grants, extends, or revokes access. A date field is display data; the provider event is the transition.
3. **IN-023 — Every row carries the provider truth.** Each subscription row stores the provider subscription ID, provider customer ID, current status, and current period end. Entitlement logic never infers state from payment history, signup date, or plan name.
4. **IN-024 — Trial terms are shown before signup.** Trial length, whether a payment method is required upfront, the price at conversion, and the conversion date appear on the signup surface. A trial converts only on those terms; terms that differ at charge time from terms shown at signup are a defect.
5. **IN-025 — Trial-end behavior is configured, never inherited.** For each plan, the missing-payment-method outcome at trial end (invoice, pause, or cancel) and the with-card outcome are set explicitly in the provider configuration. Provider defaults left in place are a finding.
6. **IN-026 — No surprise conversion.** A trial-will-end warning reaches the customer before conversion (driven by the provider's trial-will-end event where offered), naming the amount and the date. A first charge the customer could not see coming is a defect, not a conversion.
7. **IN-027 — Cancellation is a provider state change.** Cancel writes to the provider, the local mirror converges to the returned state, and the customer receives a confirmation stating what access remains and until when. Whether cancellation takes effect at period end or immediately is a per-plan configured choice, stated before the customer confirms.
8. **IN-028 — Cancellation is as easy as signup.** The cancel path lives in the same channel as signup, takes no more steps than signup, and requires no call, chat, or retention gauntlet. This is the ROSCA / FTC Act Section 5 line: a negative-option offer whose cancellation is materially harder than its enrollment is an unfair-practice risk, independent of any single rule.
9. **IN-029 — Plan changes declare their arithmetic first.** Before the customer confirms an upgrade, downgrade, or interval switch, the UI states the proration behavior and the effective date. The change is executed at the provider and mirrored; it is never simulated locally and "synced later."
10. **IN-030 — One entitlement rule, read from the mirror.** Every surface — web, API, email, export — decides access by reading the same mirrored subscription state, including the one written past_due access rule handed to dunning. No page improvises its own access check.
11. **IN-031 — Reconciliation repairs missed events.** A periodic sync re-reads live subscriptions from the provider and repairs any local row whose status or period end has drifted. Webhooks are assumed losable; drift found by a customer is a defect in this sync, not bad luck.
12. **IN-032 — Mutations are idempotent and server-side.** Create, plan change, pause, resume, and cancel are executed server-side with an idempotency key derived from the business operation, so a double-click, retry, or replayed request produces exactly one effect.

## BAN list

- **BAN-IN-011 — The UI-only cancel.** Banned: a cancel button that hides the subscription in the UI while the provider keeps billing, or that revokes access the provider still shows as paid. Defeats: DET-FAKE-011. Instead: cancel at the provider, converge the mirror to the returned state, and confirm to the customer what remains and until when (IN-027). Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-IN-012 — The timer entitlement.** Banned: granting, extending, or revoking access from a local clock, a `trialEndsAt` comparison, or a client-side plan flag. Defeats: DET-FAKE-021. Instead: entitlements read the mirrored provider state only (IN-022, IN-030). Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-IN-013 — Status ahead of the provider.** Banned: any surface displaying a subscription state the provider has not reached — "Pro active" rendered on signup success, "canceled" shown before the provider confirms. Defeats: DET-FAKE-022. Instead: render state from the mirror, which moves only on provider events or verified reads (IN-021). Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-IN-014 — The phantom plan change.** Banned: applying an upgrade or downgrade in local state only, so it shows in the app but never reaches the provider and reverts or double-charges at renewal. Defeats: DET-FAKE-016. Instead: execute the change at the provider with proration stated up front, then mirror the result (IN-029). Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-IN-015 — The subscription that exists only in your database.** Banned: marking a customer subscribed — plan, welcome email, unlocked features — without a subscription object existing at the provider. Defeats: DET-FAKE-006. Instead: create the subscription at the provider first; the local row is its mirror and carries its ID (IN-023). Severity: BLOCK.

## Gates

- **G-IN-011 — Test-clock lifecycle walk.** Verifies: IN-021, IN-025, IN-026. Check: automated — in test mode with a provider test clock, create a trialing subscription, advance the clock, and assert in order: the trial-will-end warning is sent, the conversion charge matches the terms shown at signup, a decline card moves the mirror to past_due, and a card update returns it to active. Pass: every transition lands in the configured local state. Fail: block shipment. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-IN-012 — Missed-webhook drill.** Verifies: IN-031. Check: automated — disable the webhook endpoint for one renewal cycle in test mode, let the renewal happen, re-enable the endpoint, and run the reconciliation sync. Pass: the sync repairs the mirror to the provider's state with no manual edit. Fail: block shipment; the sync is part of the feature, not an enhancement. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-IN-013 — Cancel-path verification.** Verifies: IN-027, IN-028. Check: automated plus timed walkthrough — script a cancellation in test mode and assert the provider state, the local mirror, the confirmation message, and the entitlement at period end all agree; then walk signup and cancel side by side and count steps. Pass: all four records agree and cancel takes no more steps than signup. Fail: block shipment. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-IN-014 — Trial-terms surface diff.** Verifies: IN-024, IN-025. Check: automated — extract the trial length, card requirement, conversion price, and trial-end behavior from the signup surface and diff them against the provider product/price and subscription configuration. Pass: zero differences, and both card and no-card trial-end outcomes are explicitly configured. Fail: block shipment. Recorded in: progress.md.

## Recall anchors

- The provider's state machine is the only state machine.
- No local timer ever grants, extends, or revokes access.
- Trials convert only on the terms shown at signup.
- Cancel at the provider, confirm to the customer, same steps as signup.
- Webhooks get missed; the reconciliation sync is not optional.

## Checklist

- [ ] Every subscription row carries provider subscription ID, status, and period end (IN-023).
- [ ] Trial-end behavior is explicitly configured for card and no-card cases (G-IN-014).
- [ ] Signup surface trial terms diff clean against the provider configuration (G-IN-014).
- [ ] Test-clock lifecycle walk passes end to end (G-IN-011).
- [ ] Missed-webhook drill: the sync repairs the mirror unaided (G-IN-012).
- [ ] Cancel verified at provider, mirror, confirmation, and entitlement — in no more steps than signup (G-IN-013).
- [ ] Plan-change screens state proration and effective date before confirmation (IN-029).
- [ ] All entitlement checks read the one mirrored state (IN-030).

<!-- generated from skills/integrations-payments/third-party-apis/SKILL.md (bundle form) -->

# third-party-apis

## Metadata

- **Owner department:** D11 Integrations & Payments (IN)
- **Skill version:** 1.0.0
- **Last verified:** 2026-11-21
- **Sources:** Microsoft Learn, Azure Architecture Center, "Circuit Breaker Pattern" — https://learn.microsoft.com/en-gb/azure/architecture/patterns/circuit-breaker ; Stripe, "Idempotent requests" — https://docs.stripe.com/api/idempotent_requests
- **Depends on:** api-keys-management
- **Feeds into:** payments, subscriptions, webhooks, transactional-email, sms, oauth-sso

## When to use / Do NOT use

- **Use when:** the product calls any external provider API — payments, email, SMS, maps, search, AI models, data feeds — whether adding a new integration or changing an existing one. This skill owns the wrapper every outbound call passes through.
- **Do NOT use when:** the call is to the project's own backend (api-building, D4), or the work is the provider-specific money/message semantics of a single flow (payments, webhooks, sms own those; this skill owns the shared calling discipline underneath them). Provider-specific facts live in the integration's dated annex, never in this skill.

## Rules

1. **IN-181 — One adapter per provider.** Each provider sits behind a single internal adapter module that speaks the provider's API and exposes the project's own domain interface. No provider SDK type, response object, or error shape appears outside the adapter; replacing the provider is a one-module change.
2. **IN-182 — Every call carries a timeout.** Every outbound call sets an explicit connect timeout and read timeout, sized to the caller's latency budget and recorded in the adapter's configuration. A call with no timeout is a defect, even if it has never hung yet.
3. **IN-183 — Retries are bounded and safe.** Transient failures (timeouts, 5xx, connection resets) are retried with exponential backoff and jitter, up to a configured maximum. A non-idempotent operation is retried only when it carries an idempotency key derived from the business operation; without a key it is attempted once.
4. **IN-184 — Circuit breaker per provider.** Repeated provider failures trip a circuit breaker for that provider; while open, calls fail fast into the degradation path instead of queueing behind a dead dependency. The breaker half-opens on a timer to probe recovery.
5. **IN-185 — Responses are validated before use.** Every provider response is checked against the adapter's expected schema (required fields, types, value ranges) before any field reaches domain code. A response that fails validation is an integration error, never data.
6. **IN-186 — Outage is a visible state, never empty data.** When a provider is down or a call fails after retries, the product shows its designed degradation: an explicit unavailable/stale state naming the affected feature. A provider failure is never rendered as an empty list, zero count, or "no results" — the user's data did not disappear.
7. **IN-187 — Rate limits are respected by design.** The adapter tracks the provider's documented limits (token bucket or queue where volume warrants) and treats a 429 as a backoff signal, honoring Retry-After when present. Client code never retries a 429 immediately.
8. **IN-188 — Credentials stay server-side.** Provider secret keys live in secret storage, are scoped per environment, and are used only by server-side code. The browser receives only keys the provider designed to be public, or short-lived scoped tokens the server mints. No secret appears in the client bundle, the repo, or logs.
9. **IN-189 — Contract drift alerts.** Schema-validation failures (IN-185) are logged and alerted as integration incidents, because providers change response shapes without changing version numbers. A rising validation-failure rate is treated as provider drift until proven otherwise.
10. **IN-190 — The degradation statement ships with the integration.** Every integration has a written statement, kept with its annex: what the product does when this provider is slow, down, or returning errors — which features degrade, what the user sees, and what is queued for later. No statement, no launch.
11. **IN-191 — Raw traffic is logged, secrets redacted.** Requests and responses are logged at the adapter (method, endpoint, status, latency, provider request ID) with credentials and personal data redacted, so a dispute or incident can be reconstructed from logs alone.
12. **IN-192 — Done means tested against failure.** An integration is complete only after it passes the sandbox contract suite and the failure drills (G-IN-091–G-IN-094) in staging. "It worked once in development" is not a completion state.

## BAN list

- **BAN-IN-091 — Fixture fallback sold as live.** Banned: shipping a code path that returns canned, hardcoded, or sample data when the provider call fails, times out, or was never wired up — presented to the user as the provider's real response. Defeats: DET-FAKE-009. Instead: call the provider through the adapter and surface failure per IN-186; a fallback is allowed only when it is labeled as a fallback in the UI. Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-IN-092 — Outage rendered as empty.** Banned: mapping a provider timeout, 5xx, or open circuit breaker to an empty list, zero count, or "nothing here yet" state. Defeats: DET-FAKE-022. Instead: render the degradation state from the integration's statement (IN-190) — feature unavailable, data intact, retry offered. Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-IN-093 — Swallowed errors serving stale as current.** Banned: catching provider errors and silently returning cached or default data with no staleness marker, so figures freeze while the UI claims they are live. Defeats: DET-FAKE-004. Instead: serve cached data only with a visible "as of <time>" label, or fail into the degradation state. Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-IN-094 — Success claimed before provider confirmation.** Banned: telling the user an external action succeeded (ticket created, message sent, record synced) when the request was merely dispatched, or after it failed. Defeats: DET-FAKE-010. Instead: confirm from the provider's response (or its later status callback) before claiming the effect; a pending state is shown as pending. Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-IN-095 — First page presented as the whole dataset.** Banned: fetching one page of a provider's paginated results and rendering it as the complete list, with counts, filters, or totals computed from that page alone. Defeats: DET-FAKE-017. Instead: paginate to completion or query server-side, and derive every count from the same full query as the results. Severity: BLOCK.

## Gates

- **G-IN-091 — Sandbox contract suite.** Verifies: IN-181, IN-185. Check: automated — run the adapter's contract tests against the provider's sandbox/test environment (or replayed recorded fixtures where no sandbox exists), asserting request shape, auth, pagination, and response parsing for every operation the product uses. Pass: every contract test green. Fail: block the integration change. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-IN-092 — Dead-endpoint and latency drill.** Verifies: IN-182, IN-184, IN-186. Check: automated — in staging, point the adapter at a dead URL (e.g. `http://127.0.0.1:9`) and at a fault-injection endpoint that sleeps past the read timeout; assert each affected feature answers within its latency budget with the degradation state from its statement, and that no screen renders an empty/zero state for existing data. Pass: all assertions hold. Fail: block shipment. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-IN-093 — Failure-injection retry audit.** Verifies: IN-183, IN-187. Check: automated — route the adapter through a fault proxy returning, in sequence, 500, 429 with Retry-After, and a dropped connection; assert retry count never exceeds the configured maximum, backoff intervals grow, the 429 waits at least the Retry-After interval, and a non-idempotent operation without an idempotency key is attempted exactly once. Pass: all assertions hold. Fail: block shipment. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-IN-094 — Malformed-response fixture suite.** Verifies: IN-185, IN-189. Check: automated — replay recorded provider fixtures mutated to be malformed (missing fields, wrong types, truncated body, error payload with HTTP 200) through the adapter; assert every one is rejected by schema validation, none reaches domain code, and a drift alert is emitted per case. Pass: all fixtures rejected and alerted. Fail: block shipment. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-IN-095 — Secret scan.** Verifies: IN-188. Check: automated — scan the repository and the built frontend bundle for provider key patterns (e.g. `grep -rE "(sk_live|sk_test|AKIA|ghp_)[A-Za-z0-9_]+" build/ src/` plus the project's secret-scanner in CI). Pass: zero findings. Fail: block shipment and rotate any key found. Recorded in: progress.md.

## Recall anchors

- One provider, one adapter — SDK types never escape it.
- No timeout, no call.
- Retry only what is idempotent or keyed, with backoff and a cap.
- An outage is a visible state — never empty data.
- Validate the response before a single field is used.

## Checklist

- [ ] Every provider call passes through its adapter; no SDK types leak into domain code (IN-181).
- [ ] Connect and read timeouts are configured for every outbound call (IN-182).
- [ ] Retries are bounded with backoff and jitter; non-idempotent retries carry idempotency keys (IN-183).
- [ ] Circuit breaker and degradation statement exist for this provider (IN-184, IN-190).
- [ ] Responses are schema-validated before use, and validation failures alert (IN-185, IN-189).
- [ ] Failure states render as unavailable/stale — never as empty lists or zero counts (IN-186).
- [ ] No provider secret appears in the repo, the client bundle, or logs (G-IN-095).
- [ ] Sandbox contract suite and failure drills pass in staging (G-IN-091–G-IN-094).

---

# transactional-email

## Metadata

- **Owner department:** D11 Integrations & Payments (IN)
- **Skill version:** 1.0.0
- **Last verified:** 2026-11-21
- **Sources:** Amazon SES, "Complying with DMARC authentication protocol in Amazon SES" — https://docs.aws.amazon.com/ses/latest/dg/send-email-authentication-dmarc.html ; RFC 7208 (SPF) — https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc7208 ; RFC 6376 (DKIM) — https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc6376 ; RFC 7489 (DMARC) — https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc7489 ; RFC 8058 (one-click unsubscribe) — https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8058
- **Depends on:** webhooks (provider delivery, bounce, and complaint events), api-keys-management (provider credentials)
- **Feeds into:** payments (receipts), subscriptions (billing notices), dunning (failed-payment mail), backend-auth (verification and reset mail)

## When to use / Do NOT use

- **Use when:** the product sends mail a user is waiting for because of something they just did — receipts, email verification, password resets, account and security notices, order and billing confirmations.
- **Do NOT use when:** the message is marketing or lifecycle mail — onboarding sequences, win-back, newsletters, promotional content of any kind. That is D9's lifecycle-email skill, sent on a separate stream under its own consent rules. This skill owns transactional streams only; the boundary is crossed deliberately, in a design decision, never by drift.

## Rules

1. **IN-121 — Authenticate the sending domain before the first send.** The dedicated sending subdomain publishes SPF and DKIM records aligned with the visible From: domain, plus a DMARC record that starts at `p=none` monitoring and progresses to enforcement. Alignment is proven in the `Authentication-Results` header of a real test send, not assumed from DNS records existing.
2. **IN-122 — Transactional and marketing mail use separate subdomains and streams.** A marketing reputation problem must never be able to take password resets down with it; no configuration shares a stream between the two.
3. **IN-123 — Send through a provider, as a background job.** The request handler enqueues a message with a template ID and its data; a worker sends via the email provider. No mail is sent inline in a web request, and none leaves from the app server's own SMTP.
4. **IN-124 — "Email sent" means provider-accepted, with the message ID stored.** The UI may claim a message was sent only after the provider accepts it and the returned message ID is written to the message row. Anything earlier is "sending," and a failed enqueue is an error the user sees.
5. **IN-125 — Delivery outcomes are recorded per message.** Provider delivered / bounced / complaint events return by webhook and are stored against the message row, so "did the reset email arrive" is a database query, never a guess or a support shrug.
6. **IN-126 — Bounces and complaints suppress automatically.** A hard bounce or a spam complaint adds the address to the suppression list inside the send path; no later send to that address leaves until the suppression is deliberately cleared. Re-mailing a hard-bounced address damages the domain for every user.
7. **IN-127 — Templates are versioned in the repo and ship with a plain-text part.** Every transactional template names the action it confirms or requests, the expiry where one applies, and the "this wasn't you" path. Template changes go through the same review as code.
8. **IN-128 — Templates render with tested fallbacks.** Every variable has a defined fallback for missing data; a rendered message never contains a raw template token, an empty gap, or the word "undefined". A seed-send with full and with empty data proves this before a template ships.
9. **IN-129 — Codes and links are single-use, expiring, and rate-limited.** Verification codes and reset links work once, expire on a stated clock, and are rate-limited at both send and confirm. D7 owns the security depth; this skill owns that the mechanism exists and is wired to the real send.
10. **IN-130 — Receipts and confirmations render from the stored, provider-confirmed record.** Amounts, items, and references in a receipt email come from the payment record the provider confirmed — never from template sample data, client-submitted values, or a recomputation that can drift.
11. **IN-131 — Transactional templates carry no marketing content.** No promotional block, cross-sell, or engagement bait in a transactional template: it reclassifies the stream, breaks the consent boundary with lifecycle-email, and trains filters to treat resets as bulk mail.
12. **IN-132 — A promised email that never arrives is a product defect.** Any flow that tells a user to check their inbox is verified end-to-end for arrival before launch, and failed sends retry with backoff into a visible dead-letter state — a silently dropped send is a defect, not an acceptable loss.

## BAN list

- **BAN-IN-061 — Reset toast with nothing behind it.** Banned: showing "Reset link sent" while no provider is called and no token exists. Defeats: DET-FAKE-020. Instead: enqueue a real send through the authenticated provider carrying a single-use, expiring token, and store the message ID (IN-123, IN-124, IN-129). Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-IN-062 — The staged "we emailed you" state.** Banned: notification or account state claiming an email was sent when the send is a stub, a log line, or a fixture. Defeats: DET-FAKE-013. Instead: the state is set only from the provider-acceptance record, and delivery advances only from provider events (IN-124, IN-125). Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-IN-063 — "Delivered" copied from the send response.** Banned: marking a message delivered because the provider's send API returned success. Defeats: DET-FAKE-022. Instead: acceptance records `accepted` with the message ID; only a provider delivery event records `delivered`, and bounce/complaint events record their own states (IN-125). Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-IN-064 — Receipt email rendered from sample data.** Banned: a receipt or invoice email whose amounts or items come from template placeholders or example data rather than the confirmed charge. Defeats: DET-FAKE-019. Instead: render every figure from the stored provider-confirmed payment record (IN-130). Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-IN-065 — Verification that verifies nothing.** Banned: an email-verification step that accepts any code, or marks the address verified without the code check passing. Defeats: DET-FAKE-003. Instead: the code is server-issued, single-use, and expiring; the account stays in a pending state until the real check passes (IN-129). Severity: BLOCK.

## Gates

- **G-IN-061 — Authentication check.** Verifies: IN-121, IN-122. Check: automated — query DNS (`dig +short TXT <sending-subdomain>`, the DKIM selector record, and `dig +short TXT _dmarc.<sending-subdomain>`), then send a test message and assert its `Authentication-Results` header shows SPF, DKIM, and DMARC all passing and aligned with the visible From: domain, on a subdomain separate from the marketing stream. Pass: all three pass and align. Fail: block launch; no transactional mail ships from an unauthenticated domain. Recorded in: progress.md. Simulated-provider provision (pre-provisioning): where no production sending domain or provider account exists yet, the DNS queries and header assertions run against a simulated sending setup — a test domain whose DNS records the project controls, configured exactly as the production subdomain will be, with the test send routed through it; the result is recorded as simulated in progress.md and in the product's own documentation, verification against the production sending domain remains required before launch, and simulated results must never be presented as real in any user-facing surface (Real Content Rule).
- **G-IN-062 — Seed-send token scan.** Verifies: IN-127, IN-128. Check: automated — send every transactional template to seed inboxes twice, once with complete data and once with empty optional data, and grep the rendered text and HTML parts for `{{`, `}}`, `undefined`, and `null`. Pass: zero unrendered tokens or placeholder artifacts in any rendering. Fail: block the template release. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-IN-063 — Bounce and suppression drill.** Verifies: IN-125, IN-126. Check: automated — send to the provider's bounce-simulator address; assert the message row records the bounce event and the address appears on the suppression list; then attempt a second send to the same address and assert the send path refuses it. Pass: bounce recorded, address suppressed, second send blocked. Fail: block launch. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-IN-064 — End-to-end arrival test.** Verifies: IN-123, IN-124, IN-132. Check: automated in staging — complete the signup and password-reset flows; assert a message row exists with a provider message ID and reaches the delivered state via provider events, and that completing the reset actually changes the credential (the old password fails, the new one works). Pass: both flows arrive and the reset takes effect. Fail: block launch. Recorded in: progress.md. Simulated-provider provision (pre-provisioning): where no provider account exists yet, a local simulated provider — a mail double that issues provider-style message IDs, emits delivery events, and captures the messages — stands in for the provider and both flows are verified against it unchanged; the result is recorded as simulated in progress.md and in the product's own documentation, the arrival test against the real provider remains required before public launch, and simulated results must never be presented as real in any user-facing surface (Real Content Rule).

## Recall anchors

- "Sent" means the provider accepted it and you stored the ID.
- Delivered is an event, not an assumption.
- SPF, DKIM, DMARC — aligned, or it lands in spam.
- Transactional and marketing never share a stream.
- A promised email that never arrives is a product defect.

## Checklist

- [ ] SPF, DKIM, and DMARC verified passing and aligned on a real test send (G-IN-061).
- [ ] Transactional and marketing mail are on separate subdomains and streams (IN-122).
- [ ] Every send goes through the queue and stores its provider message ID (IN-123, IN-124).
- [ ] Delivered, bounce, and complaint events are stored against each message row (IN-125).
- [ ] Hard bounces and complaints are suppressed automatically in the send path (IN-126).
- [ ] Seed-sends with full and empty data show zero unrendered template tokens (G-IN-062).
- [ ] Signup and password-reset flows verified end-to-end for arrival in staging (G-IN-064).

# webhooks

## Metadata

- **Owner department:** D11 Integrations & Payments (IN)
- **Skill version:** 1.0.0
- **Last verified:** 2026-11-21
- **Sources:** Stripe, "Receive Stripe events in your webhook endpoint" — https://docs.stripe.com/webhooks ; PROJECT_ANATOMY.md, "Webhooks"
- **Depends on:** payments, api-keys-management
- **Feeds into:** subscriptions, refunds-disputes, dunning, transactional-email

## When to use / Do NOT use

- **Use when:** a project receives provider events (payments, subscriptions, disputes, delivery status) or sends events to customers: endpoint design, signature verification, deduplication, processing, replay, and delivery logging.
- **Do NOT use when:** the question is what an event means for money state (payments and subscriptions own the semantics; this skill owns receiving and processing mechanics), or the transport is a general job queue with no provider signature or delivery contract (D4 queues-jobs owns transport mechanics).

## Rules

1. **IN-101 — Verify the signature over the raw body, before parsing.** The endpoint reads the exact bytes received and verifies the provider signature with the provider's library before any JSON parsing or body-parsing middleware touches the route. A parsed-and-reserialized body fails verification and is the most common self-inflicted outage.
2. **IN-102 — Reject and log every failed verification.** A request with a missing, invalid, or stale signature (outside the provider's timestamp tolerance — Stripe's libraries default to five minutes, the replay defense) is rejected with an error status, logged with its source, and changes no state. The endpoint is public by design; the signature is the only authentication.
3. **IN-103 — Persist before you acknowledge.** On successful verification, insert the event into an events table and only then return 2xx. The 2xx is a promise that the event is durably stored, never a claim that it has been processed.
4. **IN-104 — Deduplication is a database constraint, not a check.** The events table carries a unique constraint on the provider event ID; a duplicate delivery collides on insert and is acknowledged as already-received. An application-level "look up, then insert" is a race (DET-CODE-030), not deduplication.
5. **IN-105 — Process asynchronously, never in the request.** The request handler verifies, stores, and returns; a worker processes from the queue. No provider call, email send, or multi-table write happens inside the webhook request — slow handlers time out, and timeouts are what trigger duplicate retries.
6. **IN-106 — Handlers converge state; they never increment it.** A handler sets the mirror to the event's state ("set subscription status to `past_due`"), so a duplicate, a retry, or a replay of the same event is a no-op. A handler that adds, counts, or appends per delivery double-applies on the provider's normal at-least-once delivery.
7. **IN-107 — Assume unordered delivery.** Events arrive out of order; a handler never trusts arrival order or an older event over newer state. Where the event's object state matters, re-read the current object from the provider API and converge the mirror to that, so a late `created` event cannot resurrect a canceled subscription.
8. **IN-108 — Reconcile before fulfilling.** A signed event is necessary but not sufficient: before any fulfillment or entitlement change, the event is checked against the expected local record — account, amount, currency, and state must all match. A verified event naming the wrong amount fulfills nothing and is logged for review.
9. **IN-109 — Recover missed events with a periodic provider-state sync.** A scheduled job re-reads the provider state for active objects (subscriptions, open invoices, recent payments) and repairs the mirror where it has drifted. Webhooks get missed — endpoints go down, deliveries exhaust retries — and the sync is what makes the mirror converge anyway.
10. **IN-110 — Every delivery and outcome is logged, and failures are replayable.** Each event row records receipt time, verification result, processing outcome, and attempt count; a failed processing keeps the event and retries or dead-letters it for manual replay, never drops it. Events that arrived while the endpoint or worker was down are recovered by provider resend or event re-fetch, and the replay path is tested, not assumed.
11. **IN-111 — The signing secret is a credential.** Each endpoint has its own signing secret, held in the project's secret store (never in source, config files committed to the repo, or logs), and rotatable without a code change. D7 secrets-management owns compromise response; this skill owns the per-endpoint register entry.
12. **IN-112 — Outbound webhooks follow the same discipline.** Events sent to customers are signed with a per-endpoint secret the customer can rotate, retried with backoff over days (not minutes), logged per attempt with the response received, and exposed in a delivery-status view with a customer-triggered replay. An outbound event with no delivery record is a claim, not a notification.

## BAN list

- **BAN-IN-051 — The trusted POST.** Banned: a webhook endpoint that acts on any POST claiming an event ("payment succeeded") without signature verification. Defeats: DET-FAKE-006. Instead: verify the signature over the raw body first (IN-101) and reject failures (IN-102). Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-IN-052 — Check-then-insert deduplication.** Banned: deduplicating by reading for an existing event row and inserting if absent. Defeats: DET-CODE-030. Instead: a unique constraint on the provider event ID makes the duplicate collide safely (IN-104). Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-IN-053 — The incrementing handler.** Banned: handlers that advance state per delivery — incrementing a counter, appending a credit, counting retries as renewals. Defeats: DET-FAKE-022. Instead: handlers set the mirror to the event's state, so redelivery is a no-op (IN-106). Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-IN-054 — The swallowed processing failure.** Banned: catching a handler exception, returning 2xx anyway, and discarding the event. Defeats: DET-CODE-005. Instead: the stored event keeps a failed outcome, retries or dead-letters, and is replayable (IN-110); the failure is visible, not absorbed. Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-IN-055 — The committed signing secret.** Banned: a webhook signing secret hardcoded in source or committed in a config file. Defeats: DET-CODE-018. Instead: the secret lives in the secret store, one per endpoint, rotatable without a deploy (IN-111). Severity: BLOCK.

## Gates

- **G-IN-051 — Forgery test.** Verifies: IN-101, IN-102. Check: automated — POST a correctly shaped payment event to the endpoint with an invalid signature (and a second with a valid signature over a tampered body), then query the affected order. Pass: both requests are rejected with an error status and the order state is unchanged. Fail: block shipment. Recorded in: progress.md. Simulated-provider provision (pre-provisioning): where no provider account exists yet, the endpoint is configured with a local simulated provider's signing secret and both forgery cases are exercised against it unchanged; the result is recorded as simulated in progress.md and in the product's own documentation, the run with a real provider-issued signing secret remains required before public launch, and simulated results must never be presented as real in any user-facing surface (Real Content Rule).
- **G-IN-052 — Duplicate-delivery test.** Verifies: IN-104, IN-106. Check: automated — deliver the same real event twice through provider tooling (resend from the provider dashboard or CLI) and assert one event row, one state transition, and one side effect (one grant, one email). Pass: exactly one effect from two deliveries, including under concurrent delivery. Fail: block shipment. Recorded in: progress.md. Simulated-provider provision (pre-provisioning): where no provider account or provider tooling exists yet, a local simulated provider — a provider double that delivers validly signed events and resends the same event on demand — stands in for the provider and this check runs against it unchanged; the result is recorded as simulated in progress.md and in the product's own documentation, the run through the real provider's tooling remains required before public launch, and simulated results must never be presented as real in any user-facing surface (Real Content Rule).
- **G-IN-053 — Backlog replay test.** Verifies: IN-105, IN-109, IN-110. Check: automated — stop the worker, deliver a sequence of events (including an out-of-order pair), restart the worker, then run the provider-state sync. Pass: the mirror converges to the provider's current state, every event has a recorded outcome, and no effect is doubled. Fail: block shipment. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-IN-054 — Reconciliation-before-fulfillment test.** Verifies: IN-108. Check: automated — in test mode, deliver a validly signed event whose amount does not match the expected order, and assert nothing is fulfilled and the mismatch is logged. Pass: zero fulfillment, one logged mismatch. Fail: block shipment. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-IN-055 — Signing-secret scan.** Verifies: IN-111. Check: automated — grep the repository and committed config for signing-secret literals and provider secret prefixes (e.g. `whsec_`) and assert the endpoint reads its secret from the secret store at runtime. Pass: zero literals in the repo. Fail: block shipment and rotate the exposed secret. Recorded in: progress.md.

## Recall anchors

- Verify the signature over the raw bytes — before parsing, every time.
- Store first, acknowledge second, process third — never in the request.
- Duplicates and disorder are normal delivery, not errors; converge, don't count.
- A signed event still has to match the order before it fulfills anything.
- Missed events are certain; the periodic sync is what makes the mirror true.

## Checklist

- [ ] Signature verified over the raw body before any parsing middleware (IN-101, G-IN-051).
- [ ] Failed verifications are rejected and logged with no state change (IN-102).
- [ ] The event is durably stored before the 2xx is returned (IN-103).
- [ ] A unique constraint on the provider event ID enforces deduplication (IN-104, G-IN-052).
- [ ] Handlers set state, never increment it, and tolerate out-of-order arrival (IN-106, IN-107).
- [ ] Fulfillment reconciles account, amount, currency, and state first (IN-108, G-IN-054).
- [ ] The periodic provider-state sync runs and the replay path is tested (IN-109, IN-110, G-IN-053).
- [ ] Signing secrets are per-endpoint, in the secret store, and absent from the repo (IN-111, G-IN-055).
